summary.text:
Croydon's 2025/26 review is the most completely checkable treasury report in the library. Section 5.24 makes four claims — £285m drawn at 4.54%, £148.7m of it refinancing debt at 5.51%, a £136.3m net increase, £4.75m more interest a year — and all four rebuild exactly from the loan-by-loan table printed beneath them. The drawings sum to £285.000m and reblend to 4.5400%; the repayments sum to £148.675m and reblend to 5.5075%; the net is £136.325m; and the interest arithmetic gives £4.751m.

The PWLB book ties to our file to the pound: 79 loans outstanding at 31 March 2026, £1,468,926,000 at 3.9470%, against their £1,468.9m at 3.95%. Tables 5, 6, 7, 10, 11 and 12 all foot, as do both CFR accounts, and the balance sheet identity closes exactly — CFR £1,968.2m less £1,595.9m of external borrowing less £196.9m of other long-term liabilities is the £175.4m of CFR under-funding they print in Table 3.

Appendix B is the best rate appendix we have read. All four PWLB margins are stated correctly, including the Local Infrastructure Rate at gilt+60 through the National Wealth Fund and the HRA rate at gilt+40, and the five certainty rates quoted for 31 March 2026 match ours five for five.

The forward shape: £338m — a fifth of the book — reprices by March 2028 at a current average of about 4.93%, which today's one- and two-year certainty rates (4.95% and 5.06%) sit within a few basis points of. The long half of the book is the opposite story: 48.9% beyond ten years at an average 3.25%, which is where essentially all of the £232.6m of discount on today's repayment curve sits. Separately, £45.0m of the £65.9m investment portfolio was lent to other local authorities at 5.36% while the money market funds alongside it paid 3.82%.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the annual review that went to Audit and Governance on 25 June and Full Council on 20 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first, and an unusually complete one. We hold 83 PWLB loans for Croydon. Restricted to those outstanding at 31 March 2026 that is 79 loans and £1,468,926,000 at a weighted 3.9470%, against the £1,468.9m at 3.95% in your Table 5 — to the pound and to the basis point. The remaining four in our file were drawn after the year end. Your £127.0m of market debt is not PWLB, so it is correctly absent from our side and the two totals reconcile.

We wrote because of section 5.24, which is the reason the rest of this email is short.

That paragraph makes four claims: £285m drawn at an average 4.54%, of which £148.7m refinanced maturing debt at an average 5.51%, a net increase of £136.3m, and £4.75m more interest a year. We rebuilt all four from Table 8. The twelve drawings sum to £285.000m and reblend to 4.5400%. The twelve repayments sum to £148.675m and reblend to 5.5075%. The net is £136.325m. And £285m at 4.54% less £148.675m at 5.51% is £4.751m. Every one of them, exactly.

That is rare. Most reports state the averages and leave the reader to take them on trust, because the underlying table isn't printed. Yours is, so a member who wants to check the £4.75m can check it. Tables 5, 6, 7, 10, 11 and 12 all foot as well, both CFR accounts foot, and the balance sheet identity closes on your own figures — CFR £1,968.2m less £1,595.9m of external borrowing less £196.9m of other long-term liabilities is the £175.4m of CFR under-funding in Table 3.

Second, Appendix B, which is the best rate appendix we have read this year. It states all four PWLB margins correctly — standard at gilt plus 100, certainty at gilt plus 80, the Local Infrastructure Rate at gilt plus 60 through the National Wealth Fund, and the HRA rate at gilt plus 40 — and the five certainty rates it quotes for 31 March 2026 match our own record for that day five for five: 5.04, 5.28, 5.72, 6.29 and 6.08. Of the councils we have read this year only a handful get every margin right, and fewer still quote rates we can match on every tenor. Worth knowing that the reference points your members are being given are sound.

Third, the one forward-looking observation we would offer, and it is more reassuring than not. £268.0m of the book matures inside twelve months at an average 4.93% and another £70.0m inside two years at 4.95% — £338m, a fifth of the portfolio, repricing by March 2028. On this afternoon's notice, 314/26, the one-year certainty rate is 4.95% and the two-year 5.06%. So on the curve as it stands that £338m reprices within a few basis points of what it already costs, which is not the position most councils with a comparable short bucket are in. The interesting contrast is at the other end: 48.9% of the book sits beyond ten years at an average 3.25%, and it is that half, not the short half, that carries the whole of the discount position below.

On which — on the DMO's premature repayment curve today, 47 of your 75 live loans price below par for about £240.5m of discount, against £7.9m of premium on the 27 above, so a net discount of roughly £232.6m. The single largest is the £40m at 2.24% running to 2063, at about £20.6m. We're not suggesting anything follows from that: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote a real figure. It is simply the arithmetic consequence of having drawn a long book at rates in the twos and a curve now in the fives, and yours is priced daily at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

One smaller note. Your Table 10 shows £45.0m of the £65.9m portfolio placed with other local authorities at 5.36%, against £20.9m in money market funds at 3.82%, with Appendix D capping each authority at £10m. Across everything we have read this year, inter-authority pricing over this year end ran from about 4.45% to 8.50%, so 5.36% for a spread of maturities out to nine months sits comfortably in the middle of a very wide distribution. No council can see that distribution from its own trades, which is why we publish it. July's PWLB lending was thin — £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% — and thin PWLB months are exactly when the inter-authority market prices widest. The breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

On training, four fit Croydon. Strategic PWLB borrowing and Interest rate risk go to the £338m repricing by 2028. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets goes to the £45m of deposits. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator covers the discount position above. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/
